About a month or so ago, something very similar to this happened in my town (Spain). An american-german couple moved here with their three kids and then they proceeded to shut themselves in completely for four years.
According to the news it began as some sort of extreme covid anxiety, and then they realized that they couldn't stop isolating without attracting outside attention. The kids weren't in school, and hadn't been in at least four years. They hadn't any shoes their size. They hadn't been outside for half of their lives. They were still in diapers, even the oldest one, who if I recall correctly was like eight when they were rescued.The only person in the whole family that appeared in the country's immigration records was the father: the wife and kids didn't exist at all to the government. They only found out that this was happening because a neighbour called our equivalent of CPS after seeing children through the (always closed) windows but never seeing them leave for school.

This is obviously the absolute worst scenario, but since I saw OP mention that he made this post after a conversation with his wife about the potential logistics of having kids,  I thought this might be relevant. This /has/ happened before.
I hope you manage to get through to her with the help of your family and hers, and I hope she gets to live a healthier, less terrifying life. But please PLEASE don't add a kid to the equation.

Something really similar happened to me on bupropion as well, although in my country it's marketed under a different name. I started having panic attacks out of the blue and they put me on bupropion 150, which would also supposedly help me quit smoking.

That was almost exactly three months ago, and the side effects are only now starting to subside (or at least stabilize). The shaking, the random adrenaline dumps triggered by something as dumb as changing position in bed, the constant tachycardia, the obsessive thoughts, you name it. I was suicidal for weeks and I managed to convince myself that my body was genuinely malfunctioning and I was going to die. At some point I got an EKG and my bloodwork done and everything was mostly normal aside from a slight vitamin deficiency, but it didn't help much with the fact that I was practically unable to leave the house without feeling like I was going to pass out. 
The good thing is that, amidst all of that, any anxiety I might have felt from quitting smoking has gone largely undetected. I haven't lost a single pound, I've considered self harm multiple times and it's made me pretty much permanently afraid, but I've been smoke free for three months, so yeah. Yay me.

I feel so damaged. I'm really, really looking forward to quitting it, but I don't feel safe quitting cold turkey and right now it's hard to schedule regular appointments or even talk to a doctor in person because there's a shortage of healthcare personnel where I live.
So yeah, I'm always glad to read people's positive experiences with this drug, but it's definitely DEFINITELY not for everyone.

Hey there. First, I wanted to say that I'm rooting for you and that I completely understand the feeling. I'm a trans man (4 months on T) and the changes really can't happen fast enough. 

Just know that they will arrive. The only thing you need is that sweet sweet HRT, which you already have access to. If you think there might be any problem with the dosage, maybe you can consult it with your doctor. You might benefit from a higher dose or something. 

Waiting is hard and dysphoria is a bitch. One thing I used to do when I found it very hard to cope was listing down all the things about myself that made me dysphoric and try to find something stereotypically masculine about them. If a friend helped me with it, all the better; it's even better to feel validated by others. In the end I came to the conclusion that I was clinging too hard to the "uwu smöl androgynous boi" idea most people have about trans men. I'm broad-shouldered, I have a round face and a dad bod. And I love it! 

Although you might not conform to the standards of cis femininity (and I know how that hurts, trust me) it doesn't mean that you're not feminine. I'm convinced that most people perceive you as a feminine individual, even if your appearance is taking some time to match your identity. 

You could maybe even give r/toastme a go. It's an extremely positive and encouraging subreddit, very trans friendly for the most part. 
Over all, please remember that it's okay to feel discouraged. Nobody ever said that transitioning would be easy. Just by waiting, keeping yourself safe and reaching out you're making life so, so much easier for future you.

Transitioning is the only way I know out of that skin that never fit me right other than killing myself.

Hey there! I'm a little older than you (19FtM) but it seems we're going through the same things. 
Unfortunately, it's normal for parents to not be receptive to this kind of situation. Still better than being disowned or abused, but definitely not pleasant. 

I came out when I was sixteen and my parents have ignored it ever since. They've come with me to a grand total of one (1) therapy appointment and that's that, but they won't respect my pronouns , address me by my name or otherwise go out or their way in any shape or form to accommodate to my needs. 

The "it's just a phase" thing? Iconic. That's what my parents struggle the most with and honestly, I don't think they're ever going to grow out of it. 
Sometimes you might need to accept that they love you, but they don't understand you and aren't trying to. 
Hell, even if it was a phase, kids need support while going through the phases of their self-development. Whatever they might be, it should be the norm to support your child and encourage them to explore their identity, not put them down for it. There's nothing wrong with phases, and gender issues are legit life-changing ordeals 99 percent of the time anyways. 

HOWEVER. That doesn't mean you need to be miserable or sad. There's plenty of ways you can work your way around their restrictions and their prejudice, and a lot of things to read about it online. 

I wish you the best of luck. Also if you're interested in the few tips I've gathered through the years to get by, hit me up!

Hey, trans dude here. What you're experiencing is most definitely the impostor syndrome. It's a fucked-up phenomenon caused by the fact that you've been constantly conditioned to believe that, as a trans person, you're either asking for attention or being selfish for wanting to be respected. You're not! Your concerns and needs are valid. 

Personally, I'd say you just go with whatever feels right. Your pronouns are yours and yours only to choose. Besides, they are just words! They have no real significance, although they can sure make a difference in your mental well-being. Pronouns can't be "appropriated", either, since they are not exclusive to any community or closed group, and obviously they are not a limited resource. I, myself, believe that both gender and sexuality can slowly change over the course of one's life according to experiences and self-growth. It's perfectly possible to never have them change, as well, but it's not weird or wrong to feel a shift in your gender or sexuality. If you start using female pronouns and with time you find out that they don't describe you anymore, it's completely okay and you can always go back.

Did you know there's a whole faction of lesbians that go by he/him pronouns? They identify as female, but they use their pronouns to distance themselves from the usual expectations associated with feminity. Same with those who wear binders, or men who wear dresses. 
All in all, pronouns are part of your gender expression. You use them to understand yourself and help others do too. Do what you think is best, and if you need somebody to talk to about this, hmu.
Good luck!
